claims.text: A minor Zr addition to a refractory high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties when combined with controlled thermomechanical processing.
Hf can be used as an alternative to Zr in the proposed intervention.
The initial material is a refractory high-entropy alloy with a conventional solid-solution microstructure lacking a controlled nano-precipitate dispersion.
Tailored thermomechanical processing will induce uniform nanoscale dispersoid precipitation.
The minor Zr or Hf addition will participate in or promote formation of the proposed dispersoids.
Nano-dispersoids impede dislocation motion and thereby provide precipitation strengthening.
Nano-dispersoids pin grain boundaries and inhibit grain-boundary migration.
Inhibiting grain-boundary migration will stabilize the alloy microstructure at elevated temperature.
The intervention will increase elevated-temperature yield strength relative to a similarly composed alloy produced without the Zr addition and specialized processing.
The intervention will improve elevated-temperature creep resistance relative to the conventional baseline.
The expected improvement in elevated-temperature mechanical properties is approximately 10–20%.
The proposed effect should hold at approximately 600 °C and above.
Refractory high-entropy alloys with this intervention could be relevant to aerospace or nuclear extreme-environment applications.
The effect may not translate to lower-temperature applications.
The effect is not expected in alloy systems that do not support nanoprecipitation.
The optimal Zr concentration, processing parameters, precipitate size distribution, and quantitative property improvement remain unknown.

The proposed experiment compares an intervention group with a control lacking both the minor Zr addition and specialized thermomechanical processing, using elevated-temperature mechanical testing and TEM characterization.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement exceeding 10% in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance, or failure to confirm nano-dispersoids, would falsify the hypothesis.
